summary: A cast-iron light off Norwalk, lit in 1906 and automated in 1933: its keepers, the rescues they made, and the owners who restored it after the 2015 auction.

lens.note: Fourth-order Fresnel lens at the 1906 start (LighthouseFriends); the 1985 NRHP form describes the lantern as having lost its original apparatus

structures.note: Three stories of living space under a watchroom and lantern (NRHP)

access.note: Privately owned. Reachable by boat; tower closed; owners run art workshops and residencies by arrangement (owners' site; LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: Cockenoe Lighthouse Preservation Group, LLC (Delaware), owner since the 2015 auction

events.note: Cast-iron conical light on a cast-iron cylinder foundation; work halted July 1905 and resumed March 1906 (NRHP; LighthouseFriends)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens, two-second white flash every ten seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Congress appropriates $10,000 for a light and fog signal on Peck Ledge (3 March 1901); later estimates rise to $39,000 for a two-keeper station
Kitchen fire started by the keeper's tar pot, 17 February 1913; put out by the keeper (LighthouseFriends)
Steamship Middletown grounded on a ledge off Goose Island in fog, September 1913; passengers taken off by tugs (New England Lights, unconfirmed)

Keepers rescue four men from the sunken canal steamer J. C. Austin, of Brooklyn. Commissioner's report and Bulletin give the rescue (Bulletin dates it 5 December). The Bulletin issue reporting it is dated 3 January 1922, so the year is inferred as 1921; LighthouseFriends places the recognition in 1922.
Keeper Charles J. Kenney tows a drifting power boat to Westport, 20 August 1923
Keepers rescue two girls and two young men from an overturned canoe, 3 July 1928 (LighthouseFriends)
First assistant Oppel rescues the occupants of the catboat Eleanor, 19 May 1930
Power boat fire within a quarter mile of the light; keepers pick up a man found exhausted, 4 March 1932
Light automated over local protests; head keeper Clarke moved to Greens Ledge
USLHS roster lists three Coast Guard men at the station, 1942-1943, without roles
Coast Guard buoy tender Redwood crew replaces the light and power source and seals the tower
Redwood crew sandblasts and repaints the caisson and cleans the interior
National Register of Historic Places
Superstorm Sandy washes away the lower gallery
Coast Guard declares the light excess and offers it under the historic lighthouse preservation act
Sold at online auction (closed 15 September 2015) for $235,000 to the Cockenoe Lighthouse Preservation Group LLC
Restoration work begins under the owners
Multi-year restoration completed
Limited artist engagements and residencies with The Norwalk Art Space; access limited

corrections.why: The 1985 NRHP form gives 54 feet above mean high water at the focal plane (about 16.5 m). LighthouseFriends gives 61 feet to the lantern room (about 18.6 m), which may be the figure in the record. Check the focal plane on the Light List before changing.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NRHP: 54 feet to the focal plane. LighthouseFriends: lantern room 61 feet above the water. Record: 18.6 m. The figures may measure different things; unresolved.

The Bulletin (1922 issue) gives the Austin rescue as 5 December, and its issue contents point to December 1921. LighthouseFriends says 1922. Story follows the Bulletin for the date and notes the year as inferred.
Commissioner and Bulletin: four men rescued. New England Lights: five men. Story follows the official reports.
Bulletin 1930 names Lewis P. Oppel; USLHS roster names Percy L. Oppel for 1927-1933; LighthouseFriends names Lewis Oppel in 1932. Not resolved.

Owners' home page: Lighthouse Preservation Group, LLC. Owners' restoration page: Cockenoe Lighthouse Preservation Group, a Delaware LLC. LighthouseFriends: Cockenoe Lighthouse Preservation Group, an LLC. Story uses the Cockenoe name with the Delaware LLC form.
USLHS roster spells Louis F. Toocker; LighthouseFriends spells Louis F. Tooker. Roster spelling used.
1933 in LighthouseFriends, the owners' home page and New England Lights. Consistent.
Owners' home page: about 1 mile off the Connecticut shore. LighthouseFriends: just over two miles offshore from Calf Pasture Park. Story gives no distance.
The 1985 NRHP form describes a battery-powered green light flashing every four seconds; the record gives Fl G 2.5s. Not resolved; characteristic not used in the story.
The National Register form says 250 bags of concrete filled the foundation; LighthouseFriends says 250 bags of mortar were placed inside it. The story gives both.

The Bulletin (1923) says Keeper Kenney went out in his own power boat to a drifting power boat; LighthouseFriends says a barge captain whose leaking launch was adrift waved for help and Kenney went out in the station's launch. The story gives the Bulletin account and the LighthouseFriends account.

The USLHS roster and LighthouseFriends's 1928 account name Percy L. Oppel; the 1930 Bulletin prints Lewis P. Oppel and LighthouseFriends's 1932 report says Lewis Oppel. The story says the sources do not settle the first name.

notes_for_editor: Roster: all 36 USLHS lines entered as printed; plus Lewis P. Oppel from the 1930 Bulletin (name conflict noted). Not used in the story: a Norwich Bulletin item of 12 August 1920 (https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn82014086/1920-08-12/ed-1/?sp=1, p.1) calls William Rhodes keeper of Peck's Ledge and says he was fined $50 and costs for selling undersized lobsters. The USLHS roster does not list him and names Charles J. Kenney as head keeper that year. The Commissioner's 1920 list names a William F. Rhodes at Greens Ledge. Probably a misattribution or a different man; needs identifying before use. Not used: New England Lights' 1911 arrest of keeper Hawk and assistant Heizman for taking lobsters, and its 1914 custody dispute over an assistant. Single secondary source; personal matters. Middletown grounding (1913) rests on New England Lights alone (a secondary web guide that cites no source), and the story attributes it to that guide; a Chronicling America search for 'steamship Middletown' and 'Goose Island' in 1913 returned nothing. The 3 July 1928 canoe rescue is LighthouseFriends only; a 1928 Chronicling America search for Peck's Ledge returned nothing. A G. W. Bardwell appears in the 1918-1923 Bulletin index as keeper at Galveston Jetty; a different station, not linked. The 1921 Austin rescue: the Bulletin text 'On Decem ber 5' is quoted as OCR-broken text in the evidence; the year is inferred from the 1922 issue's date (Washington, January 3, 1922), and the story says so. New England Lights gives five men; the Commissioner and the Bulletin give four, and the story uses four. The keeper's 1913 fire is retold from LighthouseFriends; New England Lights gives a fuller version, consistent on the facts used. Owners' site and LighthouseFriends are both undated pages; re-check the access arrangements before any visit advice goes live. Names of the 1928 canoe-rescue party are not given in the source and are not invented. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the story says the Bulletin's 1923 Kenney account used his own power boat, and LighthouseFriends's station-launch account is given beside it; the 1928 Oppel and the 1930-1932 Oppel first names are left unresolved in the story; the Westport location comes from the owners' site (footnote 10). Focal height: the NRHP figure is the focal plane (54 ft / 16.5 m) and the LighthouseFriends figure is the lantern room (61 ft / 18.6 m); the story gives both and says they measure different points.
